title: Scattered People Carry the Message
overview: Violence drives the first believers out of Jerusalem, and as they flee, their message reaches Samaritans and an official from Africa.

parts.label: Stephen buried, church scattered (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: After Stephen was stoned, a wave of violence drove most believers out of Jerusalem, though the apostles stayed. Saul, who later became the apostle Paul, approved the killing and went house to house jailing men and women, something he later spoke of with deep regret.

parts.label: Philip in Samaria (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Philip, one of the seven helpers chosen in chapter 6 rather than the apostle of the same name, took the message to Samaria. Jews and Samaritans had been bitter rivals for centuries over where and how to worship God, so a joyful welcome there was striking.

parts.label: Simon the magician (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Simon had built a following through magic, and people treated him as a kind of living divine power. He was baptized too, but the story hints he was mostly dazzled by Philip's miracles.

parts.label: Peter and John visit (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: Leaders from Jerusalem came, prayed, and placed their hands on the new believers, and they received God's Spirit. Why this came later than baptism here is unclear; many readers think it showed the Samaritans fully joined the same community as the Jewish believers.

parts.label: God's gift is not for sale (vv. 18-25)
parts.note: Simon offered cash for the power to pass on the Spirit, and Peter sharply refused, saying God's gift cannot be bought and urging him to turn from this and pray. The later church named the buying of church positions "simony" after him.

parts.label: The Ethiopian official (vv. 26-40)
parts.note: On a desert road Philip met the treasurer of the queen of Ethiopia, a kingdom south of Egypt, who was a eunuch, a castrated man, and so likely limited in temple worship under the old law. He was reading Isaiah's poem about a servant who suffers in silence, which Christians read as pointing to Jesus, and Philip explained it that way and baptized him.

disagreement: Christians differ over what the delay between baptism and receiving the Spirit in Samaria means: some see a normal second experience for believers, while others see a one-time event marking the Samaritans' inclusion.
think: When something meant to shut you down ends up sending you somewhere new, how do you tell whether it was a loss, an opening, or both?
